title: reservoir-pacing-latency-cost-scan-memo
content:
Summary:

This note captures a targeted sweep comparing a 'reservoir' request-pacing strategy against a simple fixed-window pacing baseline for conversational workloads. Goal: quantify latency tail behavior (p90/p99) and incremental cost per 100k requests under different request burstiness profiles. This is exploratory — results are noisy in places and are intended to inform whether we should prototype a reservoir-style admission controller in the fast-path.

Motivation:
- Windowed pacing (fixed short time-slices) is simple but can create short-lived amplification under uneven arrival patterns, increasing p99.
- Reservoir pacing: maintain a token budget reservoir that refills at a steady rate; allow immediate admission while ensuring long-term average slot consumption is bounded. Hypothesis: reservoir reduces extremes in tail latency for mixed session-length workloads while keeping amortized GPU utilization similar.

Testbed & methodology:
- Cluster: 8x A100-40GB dedicated inference nodes (identical config), model: open-llama-13B-quant, batcher: continuous batching enabled, kv-cache enabled.
- Load generator: synthetic conversation generator producing sessions with inter-arrival distributions: (1) steady Poisson (lambda=200 qps), (2) spiky compound Poisson (bursts with mean 1s length, peak 1200 qps), (3) heavy-tailed session lengths (Pareto alpha=1.8).
- Duration: each run 30 minutes, warmup 5 minutes. Each scenario repeated 3x.
- Pacing configs:
  - windowed-10ms: fixed 10ms admission window, up to N requests per window.
  - windowed-20ms: fixed 20ms.
  - reservoir-r0.8: reservoir with refill = target_qps * 0.8, borrow cap = 2x refill, recovery smoothing 200ms.
  - reservoir-r1.0: refill = target_qps * 1.0, borrow cap = 3x.
- Metrics collected: p50/p90/p95/p99 overall latency (in ms), request drop rate, average tokens/sec per GPU, estimated cost ($) using internal cost model (normalized to $ per 100k requests).

Key numbers (aggregated medians across repeats):

Scenario A: Steady Poisson (200 qps target)
| config           | p50(ms) | p90(ms) | p95(ms) | p99(ms) | drops(%) | cost($/100k) |
|------------------|---------|---------|---------|---------|----------|--------------|
| windowed-10ms    | 65      | 112     | 160     | 280     | 0.0      | 14.8         |
| windowed-20ms    | 70      | 118     | 170     | 295     | 0.0      | 14.6         |
| reservoir-r0.8   | 68      | 110     | 148     | 210     | 0.0      | 14.9         |
| reservoir-r1.0   | 66      | 108     | 142     | 195     | 0.0      | 15.1         |

Scenario B: Spiky compound bursts (peaks ~1200 qps)
| config           | p50(ms) | p90(ms) | p95(ms) | p99(ms) | drops(%) | cost($/100k) |
|------------------|---------|---------|---------|---------|----------|--------------|
| windowed-10ms    | 120     | 450     | 760     | 1850    | 2.7      | 19.9         |
| windowed-20ms    | 130     | 410     | 640     | 1400    | 1.8      | 19.1         |
| reservoir-r0.8   | 110     | 220     | 340     | 620     | 0.5      | 20.7         |
| reservoir-r1.0   | 108     | 190     | 270     | 420     | 0.3      | 21.4         |

Scenario C: Heavy-tailed session lengths
| config           | p50(ms) | p90(ms) | p95(ms) | p99(ms) | drops(%) | cost($/100k) |
|------------------|---------|---------|---------|---------|----------|--------------|
| windowed-10ms    | 80      | 210     | 360     | 980     | 1.1      | 16.2         |
| windowed-20ms    | 84      | 200     | 330     | 820     | 0.9      | 16.0         |
| reservoir-r0.8   | 78      | 160     | 230     | 420     | 0.2      | 16.8         |
| reservoir-r1.0   | 76      | 150     | 210     | 360     | 0.1      | 17.2         |

Textual charts (ascii) - p99 comparison (lower is better):
Scenario B p99 (ms):
windowed-10ms  : |||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||| (1850)
windowed-20ms  : |||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||| (1400)
reservoir-r0.8 : |||||||||||||||||||||||||||| (620)
reservoir-r1.0 : ||||||||||||||||||||||| (420)

Cost vs p99 scatter snapshot (normalized): each line = config -> (cost, p99)
- windowed-10ms -> ($19.9, 1850ms)  [high tail, moderate cost]
- windowed-20ms -> ($19.1, 1400ms)  [slightly better tail, similar cost]
- reservoir-r0.8 -> ($20.7, 620ms)   [much improved tail, +4% cost]
- reservoir-r1.0 -> ($21.4, 420ms)   [best tail, +7% cost]

Observations / interpretation:
- Reservoir pacing consistently compresses the tail under bursty arrivals, reducing p99 by ~2.5–4x in the spiky scenario compared to windowed-10ms.
- The cost model shows a modest uplift for reservoir configs (~4–7% increase per 100k requests) in bursty tests. This is driven by slightly higher average tokens-in-flight (reservoir allows short-term oversubscription) and more frequent small batches that reduce batching efficiency in tight spikes.
- Under steady load differences are negligible: reservoir does not meaningfully harm latency or cost when arrivals are well behaved.
- Drop rates fall substantially with reservoir under spikes (from low-single-digit percent to <1%), which is important for reliability/SLA.

Risks and caveats:
- The cost model is simplified: we used static amortized GPU cost + token accounting. We did not model multi-tenant interference or preemption priority effects. Real pricing for Dedicated reservations could change the tradeoff.
- Implementation complexity: reservoir requires a global or sharded token accounting plane. Sharding choices affect fairness and risk of local exhaustion — we tested a centralized controller in this sweep.
- Workload realism: synthetic bursts approximate, but we should validate against replayed production traces (need access to sampled request traces with privacy filtering).

Recommendations:
1) Ship a lightweight prototype of reservoir pacing as an opt-in admission controller behind a feature flag for a single region; instrument p50/p95/p99 and batching efficiency over 2 weeks using canary traffic (start at 5% of traffic).
2) Add an accounting hook to the cost analyzer that attributes "short-term oversubscription tax" so we can monitor the incremental dollars driven by reservoir borrow events.
3) Run trace-replay experiments using sanitized production traces (INF-8342 is the ticket to obtain filtered traces).
4) Explore a hybrid: reservoir with an adjustable borrow cap that automatically scales during known surge windows (e.g., can be reduced when cost targets are hit).

Next steps / action items:
- Riley: prototype a sharded reservoir allocator (spike-proto branch) and instrument per-shard borrow counters. Target PR in 2 weeks.
- Aisha: add replay pipeline job to sanitize and replay a 24h production sample into the benchmark harness (blocking: data access approval).
- Marco: estimate engineering effort for an HA control plane and draft Confluence design (link in linked_artifacts) by EOD 2026-06-17.

Appendix: quick command snippets used for the run
- start generator: ./bench/generator --profile spiky --duration 30m --target 200 --seed 42
- launch controller: ./controller --mode reservoir --refill 160 --borrow-cap 320 --smoothing 200ms
- collect metrics: ./tools/collect --prom-url $PROM --labels run=reservoir-spike-20260603 --out metrics-run.json

Open questions:
- What is the operational sweet spot for borrow-cap vs cost uplift on multi-tenant Dedicated clusters?
- How does reservoir interact with preemption/reserved capacity policies?
- Are there simple heuristics to reduce oversubscription-induced batching inefficiency (e.g., small-batch coalescing delay)?

This is a draft — comments welcome, especially on further trace sources and on whether to prioritize reservoir work ahead of other admission improvements.
